rules.text: A perfect form connects an action or a state to a later point in time: up to now, or up to a point in the past. It does not mean the action is finished.
'Before admission' is a fixed point in the past. For this sentence choose the simple past or the past perfect, not the present perfect.
Finished in the past: simple past. Started in the past and still true now: present perfect. A fact about now: present simple.

rules.text: 'For' gives the length of the period. 'Since' gives the point when it started.
The end of the period decides the tense. A finished period takes the simple past. A period up to now takes the present perfect.

rules.text: Verbs like start, begin, initiate, commence and finish name one point in time. With a finished date, use the simple past.
When in, on or at points to a date in the past, use the simple past.
Small words are easy to forget when you write quickly. A missing a is marked as an error.
From is not a time word here. Do not write from 5 years or from 2013.
6 months is a length of time. Since does not go with a length of time.
Use a comma only where you are sure. A wrong comma counts as a grammar mistake.
Use the simple past for a finding taken on a particular date. There is no progression here.
If you are not sure the reader will know a short form, write it in full: 'coronary artery disease', not 'CAD'.
Unless the case notes say the symptom has gone, use the simple present for symptoms that have not changed.
